title: Requests, limits and QoS
summary: Tell the scheduler what you need and the kernel what you may use.

steps.title: Requests and limits
body: cpu: 250m        # 0.25 of a core: used for SCHEDULING
- **requests** are what the scheduler reserves. A node with 4 CPU fits pods whose CPU *requests* add up to at most ~4 (minus system reserve), regardless of actual use.
- **limits** are enforced at run time by the kernel (cgroups). CPU over the limit is **throttled** (slow, not killed). Memory over the limit gets the container **killed**: `OOMKilled`, exit code 137.
CPU units: `1` = one core, `500m` = half a core (m = millicores). Memory: `Mi`/`Gi` (binary) or `M`/`G` (decimal).
No requests at all means the scheduler thinks the pod needs nothing, so it can pack too many onto one node.

steps.prompt: A container's memory use grows past its `limits.memory`. What happens?
options: The kernel kills it (OOMKilled, exit code 137) and the kubelet restarts it
It is throttled and slows down
The pod is moved to a bigger node
steps.explain: CPU is compressible (throttling); memory is not. Repeated OOM kills show up as `CrashLoopBackOff` with `Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled` in `kubectl describe pod`.

steps.title: QoS classes
body: From requests and limits, Kubernetes gives each pod a **Quality of Service** class. When a node runs out of memory, the kubelet evicts lower classes first.
| **Guaranteed** | every container has CPU and memory limits, and requests equal limits | last |
| **Burstable** | at least one request or limit set, but not Guaranteed | middle |
| **BestEffort** | no requests or limits anywhere | first |

If you set only a limit, the request defaults to the limit. Many teams set memory request = limit (predictable) and CPU request without a CPU limit (avoids throttling). `kubectl describe pod` shows `QoS Class`.

items: requests cpu 500m mem 1Gi, limits cpu 500m mem 1Gi
limits cpu 1 mem 512Mi only (requests default to limits)

steps.prompt: A Java service keeps restarting. `kubectl describe pod` shows the last state. Fill in the `Reason`.
steps.explain: Exit code 137 = 128 + 9 (SIGKILL). Either raise the memory limit or make the runtime respect it (`-XX:MaxRAMPercentage` for Java; .NET honours cgroup limits automatically, and `DOTNET_GCHeapHardLimit` can tighten it).

steps.prompt: A node has 4 CPU allocatable. Pods already on it request 3500m in total but are using only 1 CPU. A new pod requests 1 CPU. Can it be scheduled there?
options: No: scheduling uses requests, and only 500m is unrequested
Only if it has no limits
steps.explain: The scheduler never looks at actual usage. Over-generous requests waste capacity; too-small requests cause noisy neighbours and evictions.

steps.title: Set requests and limits, read the QoS class
prompt: This terminal runs a **real one-node Kubernetes 1.37 cluster** (k3s) with `kubectl` (alias `k`). `api` and `worker` run with no requests or limits: `kubectl get pods -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,QOS:.status.qosClass`
shows `BestEffort`, the first pods the kubelet evicts when the node runs short.
1. Give `api` the **Guaranteed** class: requests equal to limits, `250m` CPU and `128Mi` memory.
2. Give `worker` the **Burstable** class: requests of `100m` CPU and `64Mi` memory, and a memory limit of `256Mi`.

checks.name: api is Guaranteed with 250m / 128Mi
checks.cmd: kubectl rollout status deploy/api --timeout=30s >/dev/null && kubectl get pods -l app=api -o json | jq -j '[.items[] | select(.metadata.deletionTimestamp == null and .status.phase == "Running")] | sort_by(.metadata.creationTimestamp) | last | .status.qosClass' && kubectl get deploy api -o jsonpath=' {.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources.requests.cpu} {.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources.limits.memory}'
checks.fail: `api`'s pods should be `Guaranteed`: requests = limits for both CPU and memory (`250m`, `128Mi`).

checks.name: worker is Burstable
checks.cmd: kubectl rollout status deploy/worker --timeout=30s >/dev/null && kubectl get pods -l app=worker -o json | jq -j '[.items[] | select(.metadata.deletionTimestamp == null and .status.phase == "Running")] | sort_by(.metadata.creationTimestamp) | last | .status.qosClass' && kubectl get deploy worker -o jsonpath=' {.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources.requests.memory} {.spec.template.spec.containers[0].resources.limits.memory}'
checks.fail: `worker` should request `100m`/`64Mi` with a `256Mi` memory limit (Burstable).

hints: Guaranteed needs requests = limits for **both** resources in every container; anything less with some request is Burstable.
steps.explain: Requests are what the scheduler reserves; limits are what the kernel enforces (CPU is throttled, memory over the limit is OOM-killed). The QoS class falls out of them and decides eviction order under node pressure: BestEffort first, Guaranteed last. Many teams set a memory limit equal to the request and no CPU limit, avoiding throttling while keeping memory predictable.
